NODE.title: Define the minimal end-to-end path
NODE.QUESTION: What must Realm do end to end, which parts of the spec are fixed requirements (Podman rootless, OpenShell inside the container, AgentOS on OpenShell, Anda reached from the TypeScript client, the six-state machine, fail-closed filesystem and egress rules, the Omp status bar label) and which are open decisions, and what is the smallest vertical slice (realm up reaches active, realm down leaves no orphan container) that proves the architecture before breadth is added?
NODE.RATIONALE: 1. Fixed requirements: Podman rootless with no privileged mode and no host socket mount; OpenShell inside the container, with all agent execution routed through it; AgentOS via its supported API only; Anda reached from TypeScript; the six states; fail-closed file mutation in required mode; "realm active" and "realm disconnected" labels. 2. Open decisions: AgentOS identity (Rivet actor or separate product); Anda boundary (TypeScript-native or Rust shim); default policy mode; one container per session or per workspace; Omp manifest and status API; Node or Bun; Podman machine target. Each sits behind an adapter interface so the slice can start before these are resolved. 3. Required chain for the slice: CLI realm up, then Realm core, then a Podman rootless run of a digest-pinned image, then OpenShell started inside it, then an AgentOS health probe, then an Anda version handshake, then active. realm down reverses this: stopping, container removed, disconnected. 4. Tension: active requires a healthy Anda bridge, so the slice must include a minimal Anda handshake or the state rules must change. Keep the spec and build the handshake, since it is small and is the failure path that degraded exists for. 5. "Disconnected" is a display label, not a listed state; it covers unbound, connecting, and error. Model the six states internally with a reason field and map them to the two labels in one place, so the CLI, tests, and future status bar share a single source. 6. Include cheap, hard-to-retrofit hardening in the slice: digest pin, dropped capabilities, read-only root with tmpfs, CPU, memory, and PID limits, default-deny egress, a token-guarded control channel, and an on-disk session record. Defer file locks, atomic writes, MCP/ACP, and the Omp plugin. 7. Slice acceptance: with Podman present, up reaches active and down leaves zero containers carrying the realm label; with Podman absent, up returns disconnected with reason podman-missing and exits within budget; a crash mid-up is reaped on the next start.
NODE.CONCLUSION:
Minimal end-to-end path: host CLI, then Realm TypeScript core, then a Podman rootless container (digest-pinned), then OpenShell, then AgentOS, then the Anda handshake, then state active. Teardown reverses the order and must leave no container with the realm label.
Build the vertical slice first: up, down, status, and doctor in the CLI only, with the Rivet, OpenShell, and Anda adapters behind interfaces so each can be swapped once its documentation is read and recorded.
Include in the slice: digest pin, dropped capabilities, read-only root with tmpfs, resource limits, default-deny egress, token-guarded control channel, on-disk session record, and startup reaping.
Defer: advisory file locks, atomic write path, MCP and ACP surfaces, the Omp plugin and status bar, and any Rust shim unless the Anda spike forces one.
Record these decisions before the final plan: AgentOS identity, Anda boundary, default policy mode, and container granularity. Tentative defaults: advisory mode by default with fail-closed as opt-in, per the spec; TypeScript-native Anda only if its docs confirm a supported boundary.

NODE.title: Stress-test the fail-closed guarantees
NODE.QUESTION: What are the highest-risk failure modes for a sandbox that must fail closed: path traversal and symlink races between canonicalization and write (TOCTOU), lock bypass by non-cooperating writers, credential leakage into audit logs or the image, egress bypass through DNS, IPv6, or host networking, orphaned containers after a daemon crash, Omp autostart blocking the UI or exceeding its startup budget, and silent fallback to unsandboxed mutation when disconnected? For each, state the mitigation in the design and the specific test (file under test/) that proves it.
NODE.RATIONALE: 1. Enumerate the seven failure modes named in the node question and treat each as a fail-closed invariant that needs a design mitigation and a test. 2. TOCTOU: canonicalize paths against a pinned root file descriptor, open each component with O_NOFOLLOW, and write via same-directory temp file, fsync, then rename, so a swapped symlink between check and open is rejected. 3. Lock bypass and credential leakage: advisory locks only bind cooperating writers, so realm writes must re-check hash and mtime before rename. Credential-shaped paths are denied by default, and audit redaction runs before any JSONL append. 4. Egress: the container gets no network by default, IPv6 is disabled, and host networking is rejected during config validation. DNS and the exact enforcement mechanism must be confirmed against the OpenShell docs before the test is written. 5. Orphans and autostart: the session record is written before container create, orphans are reaped by label at startup, and Omp startup runs detached, raced against a budget timer that settles to disconnected(reason=budget). 6. Silent fallback: every mutating tool checks that state is active. In required mode a non-active state returns a structured error; in advisory mode it returns the write with a visible warning. 7. Map each mitigation to a file under test/ and list the unverifiable items (host-native writes, OpenShell egress mechanism) as open questions rather than facts.
NODE.CONCLUSION:
Risks and mitigations (test in brackets): - TOCTOU: pin root fd, open each component with O_NOFOLLOW, temp+fsync+rename. [test/fs/toctou.test.ts] - Lock bypass: realm writes re-check hash before rename and return LOCK_CONFLICT. [test/fs/lock.test.ts] - Credential leakage: deny credential paths, redact before JSONL append, inject no host env. [test/audit/redaction.test.ts, test/fs/deny-credentials.test.ts] - Egress (DNS, IPv6, host net): default-deny, IPv6 off, host networking rejected at config load. [test/runtime/egress.test.ts] - Orphans: session record before create; reap by label at startup. [test/session/reap.test.ts] - Autostart stall: detached start raced against budget timer, settles to disconnected(budget). [test/omp/autostart-budget.test.ts] - Silent fallback: mutating tools require active; required mode errors, advisory mode warns. [test/core/fail-closed.test.ts]
Open questions: - Can Omp intercept host-native write/edit tools? Default: no; flag those writes as residual risk. - Should required mode also gate reads? Default: gate writes only. - Is egress enforced by OpenShell policy or a proxy? Default: whatever the docs confirm, else deny all.

NODE.title: Compare architecture-shaping options
NODE.QUESTION: For the three choices that shape the architecture, compare the options and recommend one for each: (a) the Anda boundary (process protocol, JSON-RPC over stdio or socket, HTTP, WASM, or a minimal Rust shim) judged on TypeScript verifiability, version handshake, and reconnection; (b) the host-to-daemon control channel (user-only Unix socket versus loopback port with a per-session token) judged on security against other local users and on Windows-out-of-scope simplicity; (c) container granularity (per session versus per workspace) judged on lock model, orphan reaping, and the future Swarm seam. Mark which recommendations would change if the open questions in n3 resolve differently.
NODE.RATIONALE: 1. No documentation has been read in this session, so Anda, Rivet, OpenShell, and Podman behaviour is unverified; each option is judged on its criteria, not on claimed APIs. 2. For Anda TypeScript verifiability, JSON-RPC over stdio or a socket, or HTTP, can be exercised from Node with no extra toolchain if documented; WASM needs a loader; a Rust shim adds a second build and test path. 3. For Anda handshake and reconnection, a version handshake works on any transport, but stdio ties the connection to the child process lifetime, while socket or HTTP connections can be re-established under bounded backoff with jitter. 4. The Anda recommendation is a TypeScript client over the first boundary the Anda docs confirm, preferring socket JSON-RPC or HTTP, with a Rust shim only if no TypeScript-reachable surface is documented. 5. For control channel security, a user-only Unix socket (directory 0700, socket 0600) excludes other local users by filesystem permission, whereas a loopback port with a per-session token is reachable by any local process that can read the token. 6. For control channel simplicity, Windows is out of scope so no socket fallback is needed, and a socket path avoids port collisions; the token variant adds token generation, storage, rotation, and redaction work. 7. For container granularity, one container per session keeps the advisory lock table in the daemon with one owner lifetime and reaps by session record, while per-workspace needs cross-session lock leases and refcounted reaping. 8. For the Swarm seam, per-session containers let subagents share the session lock table without new isolation, and the Anda, channel, and granularity picks change only if n3 resolves the boundary, AgentOS identity, or granularity differently.
NODE.CONCLUSION: Anda boundary: TypeScript client over the first documented surface Anda Engine exposes, preferring socket JSON-RPC or HTTP. Version handshake on connect; bounded exponential backoff with jitter on reconnect. Rust shim only if no TypeScript-reachable surface is documented, kept minimal in src/anda/native/. Flips to shim if the n3 spike finds nothing documented. Control channel: user-only Unix socket (directory 0700, socket 0600) under the realm state directory. Loopback port with per-session token only as a fallback. Never mount the socket or any Podman or Docker socket into the container. Granularity: one container per session. Advisory locks live in the daemon, keyed by canonical path. Reaping keys off the session record. Flips to per-workspace only if n3 chooses it; then locks need cross-session leases and reaping needs refcounts. Unchanged across n3 outcomes: the control channel and per-session granularity. The Anda boundary changes only on the spike result; AgentOS identity affects the runtime port, not these picks.

NODE.title: Fix the shared contracts
NODE.QUESTION: What exact shared contracts must every module code against before parallel work starts: the state machine transition table for unbound, connecting, active, degraded, error and stopping (including which transitions are rejected); the typed error code catalogue with machine-readable codes; the JSON schemas for exec (argv array, shell opt-in only), read, write-with-lock, list directory, realm status and realm retry; the session record schema on disk; and the policy file schema covering workspace roots, credential-path allowlist, egress allowlist, and fail-closed or advisory mode? Name the file each lives in under src/contract/ or src/core/.
NODE.RATIONALE: 1. Enumerate the consumers from the n2 module map (core, session, audit, fs, runtime, anda, contract, mcp, acp, omp, cli). Every module that touches state, errors, tools, or persisted records must import these contracts, so they are frozen before wave 1 starts. 2. Derive the state transition table from the STATES spec and the n4 decisions. unbound to connecting to active is the forward path, degraded is a side state of active, error is reachable from connecting, active, and degraded, error to connecting is the only retry edge, and stopping returns to unbound. Every other edge is rejected. 3. Build the error catalogue from every FAILURE_CASES and GRACEFUL_DEGRADATION row, giving each a machine-readable code and a retryable flag, so modules do not invent ad hoc strings. 4. Map each of the six tools (exec, read, write-with-lock, list, status, retry) to one schema in tools.schema.json. Use argv-first exec, gate shell mode behind policy.shellEnabled, and reject unknown keys, so validation runs before any call reaches the sandbox. 5. Derive the session record and policy schemas from n4 (one container per session, user-only control socket, daemon-held locks keyed by canonical path) and from the policy requirements (mode, workspace roots, credential deny, egress allowlist). Exclude token and secret fields. 6. Check the frozen contracts against the acceptance criteria. Confirm that each rejection path has a code, each disconnected state is representable in the status view, and each schema can reject a bad input before the sandbox sees it. Then run the type checker and the state-table unit tests before wave 1 begins.
NODE.CONCLUSION: Freeze before wave 1. Modules import these and never redefine them. - src/core/states.ts: unbound, connecting, active, degraded, error, stopping. Allowed: unbound>connecting; connecting>active|error|stopping; active>degraded|error|stopping; degraded>active|error|stopping; error>connecting|stopping; stopping>unbound. Else REALM_INVALID_TRANSITION. - src/core/errors.ts: typed RealmError {code, reason, retryable}. Codes: REALM_UNBOUND, REALM_NOT_ACTIVE, REALM_STOPPING, REALM_INVALID_TRANSITION, STARTUP_BUDGET_EXCEEDED, TOOL_TIMEOUT, PODMAN_MISSING, PODMAN_MACHINE_DOWN, OPENSHELL_START_FAILED, AGENTOS_CRASH_LOOP, ANDA_UNREACHABLE, ANDA_VERSION_MISMATCH, POLICY_DENIED, PATH_ESCAPE, CREDENTIAL_PATH_DENIED, LOCK_CONFLICT, WRITE_NOT_ATOMIC, EGRESS_DENIED, SHELL_NOT_ALLOWED, SCHEMA_INVALID. - src/contract/tools.schema.json: exec {argv[]} or {shell:true, script} if policy.shellEnabled; read {path, maxBytes}; write {path, content, ifMatchSha256?} locks per call; list {path, depth}; status and retry {}. No extra keys; paths workspace-relative. - src/contract/session-record.schema.json: realmId, sessionId, workspaceRoot, state, containerId, controlSocketPath. No secrets. - src/core/policy.schema.json: mode advisory(default)|fail-closed, workspaceRoots, credentialAllow globs (credential paths denied by default), egressAllow [{host, port}], shellEnabled false, startupBudgetMs, toolQueueMs.

NODE.QUESTION: For each external source (Rivet for AgentOS, Podman, NVIDIA OpenShell, Anda, the Omp plugin and status API, the MCP specification and its transport, the ACP specification and its transport, and the Node or Bun runtime constraints of each host), which specific questions must be answered from the official documentation, with the URL and read date recorded in docs/integration/<name>.md, before which module may write integration code? Also state which tests can run with no dependency present so that wave 1 is not blocked on documentation.
NODE.RATIONALE: 1. Gate Rivet first: read rivet.dev/docs to confirm whether AgentOS is a Rivet actor service or a separate product, and record its lifecycle API in docs/integration/agentos.md with URL and read date. This blocks src/runtime/agentos.ts. 2. Gate Podman and OpenShell: from docs.podman.io and the NVIDIA OpenShell docs, confirm the rootless flags for capability drop, read-only root, tmpfs, CPU, memory and PID limits, and egress control, plus OpenShell's launch-inside-container and policy model. Record in docs/integration/podman.md and docs/integration/openshell.md. This blocks src/runtime/podman.ts and openshell.ts. 3. Gate Anda: from the Anda repository and docs, identify the supported Engine boundary (socket JSON-RPC, HTTP, or WASM), its version handshake, and whether a Rust shim is needed. Record in docs/integration/anda.md. This blocks src/anda/ and rust/. 4. Gate the Omp plugin surface: locate the Omp plugin docs (URL not supplied, so record the one found), and confirm the manifest format, lifecycle hook names, and status-bar API. Record in docs/integration/omp.md. Any sibling manifest format in the session takes precedence. This blocks plugin/. 5. Gate the protocol surfaces: confirm the MCP spec version and transport, and the ACP spec version and transport, from their official docs. Record in docs/integration/mcp.md and docs/integration/acp.md. This blocks transport code in src/mcp/ and src/acp/; shared contract types may proceed. 6. Gate host runtime constraints: for Omp, Muse Code, Claude Code, Grok Build, and Hermes Agent, record each host's Node or Bun requirement, plugin, MCP, and ACP loading model, and capability gaps in docs/integration/hosts.md. This blocks the engines field and build target. 7. Mark the no-dependency wave: policy engine, state machine transitions (including rejected ones), path canonicalization and symlink escape, schema validation, lock manager, atomic write with interrupt simulation, audit redaction, MCP and ACP contract tests against an in-memory fake ExecutionService, and doctor with mocked probes. None of these need a documentation read. 8. Enforce the gating rule: no module writes integration code until its gate file exists with URL, read date, and answered questions. An unanswered question is recorded as "not documented", and the n3 default applies. No integration code is written from memory.
NODE.CONCLUSION:
Six doc gates, each writing only its own file under docs/integration/, so the reads can run in parallel: - agentos.md (Rivet): actor service or separate product, lifecycle API. Blocks src/runtime/agentos.ts. - podman.md and openshell.md: rootless hardening flags, resource limits, egress control, OpenShell launch and policy model. Blocks src/runtime/podman.ts and openshell.ts. - anda.md: supported Engine boundary, version handshake, Rust shim need. Blocks src/anda/ and rust/. - omp.md: plugin manifest, lifecycle hooks, status-bar API. Blocks plugin/. Sibling format wins if one exists. - mcp.md and acp.md: spec version and transport. Block transport code only. - hosts.md: Node or Bun constraints and plugin, MCP, and ACP loading per host. Blocks the engines field and build target.
Wave 1 needs no documentation: policy engine, state machine, canonicalization, schema validation, lock manager, atomic write, audit redaction, contract tests against an in-memory fake ExecutionService, and doctor with mocked probes.
An unanswered gate is recorded as "not documented" and the n3 default applies.

NODE.title: Ordered execution plan in waves

Each wave lists file-disjoint units; each unit names the files it owns under ~/src/repos/agent-realm/, the change to make, and the verification commands (for example npm run typecheck, npm test, npm run test:integration gated on podman availability, and a manual status-bar check across disconnected, connecting, active and error). Wave 0 covers scaffolding, lint and test runner config, and the docs/integration notes. Later waves cover the policy and state-machine core, the filesystem lockdown, the runtime adapters, the Anda bridge spike with its recorded decision, the Omp plugin, the shared tool contract with MCP and ACP contract tests, and the CLI with doctor. For each clarification from n3 that blocks a unit, state the question to ask the user and the default to use if no answer arrives.
NODE.RATIONALE: 1. Read the n3 blockers (AgentOS identity, Anda boundary, default policy mode, container granularity, Omp manifest, macOS target, Node or Bun) and give each a default so no unit stalls on an unanswered question. 2. Freeze the shared contracts (states, errors, tool and session schemas) in Wave 0 alongside the six documentation gates, so every Wave 1 module imports fixed types and needs no external docs. 3. Put the pure core in Wave 1: policy engine, state machine, filesystem lockdown (canonicalization, advisory locks, atomic write), schema validation, audit redaction, and the runtime seam with an in-memory fake. 4. Add the runtime adapters (Podman, OpenShell, AgentOS), the Anda bridge spike, and the lifecycle controller in Wave 2, with fail-closed behavior tested against the fake before any real container runs. 5. Deliver the CLI, doctor probes, host snippets, and docs in Waves 5 and 6. File ownership is disjoint within each wave, and the final Verify line maps to the acceptance criteria.

Ask (default applies if unanswered): AgentOS actor service or separate product? Default: ExecutionService interface, no actor design. Anda TypeScript client or Rust shim? Default: TypeScript over the boundary anda.md confirms. Default policy mode? Default: advisory with visible warning; fail-closed when required mode is set. One container per session or per workspace? Default: per session. Omp manifest and status API? Default: adapter module in plugin/omp; sibling format wins if one exists. macOS and Podman machine target? Default: Linux only in v1. CLARIFICATION.QUESTION: Should Realm default to advisory or fail-closed when realm is disconnected and a file-mutating tool is called?
CLARIFICATION.WHY: Determines whether writes proceed unsandboxed with a warning or return a structured error, which changes the controller, dispatcher, and default policy file.

OPTIONS.OPTION: Advisory with warning — Writes proceed while disconnected and the status bar warns. Lowest friction, but mutations can land outside the sandbox.
Fail-closed by default — Mutating tools return REALM_NOT_ACTIVE while disconnected. Strongest guarantee, but a Podman outage blocks all edits until realm recovers.
Fail-closed for writes only — Reads stay available while disconnected, and every write is rejected. Keeps the session usable without allowing unsandboxed mutation.

CLARIFICATION.QUESTION: Should the first delivery be the vertical slice (realm up, down, status, doctor on the core and runtime), or the full in-scope list in one pass?
CLARIFICATION.WHY: A slice-first plan defers the Omp plugin, MCP, ACP, and file locks, which changes the milestones and what is verified first.

OPTIONS.OPTION: Vertical slice first — Ship up/down/status/doctor with the sandbox hardening and state machine, then add the plugin, MCP, ACP, and lock layers. Proves the architecture early.
Full scope in one pass — Build every in-scope item before the first verified release. Larger, slower, and riskier to review in one go.

CLARIFICATION.QUESTION: Should Realm run one container per agent session or one container per workspace?
CLARIFICATION.WHY: This sets how locks, orphan reaping, and the Swarm seam are modeled. Per-session is the default and is reversible, but the choice affects future subagent design.

OPTIONS.OPTION: One container per session — Simple lifetime and reaping keyed to the session record. Subagents in one session share a lock table with no extra isolation.
One container per workspace — Several sessions can share a warm container and its state. Requires cross-session lock leases and refcounted reaping.

CLARIFICATION.QUESTION: When realm is required, should Omp's built-in write and edit tools be disabled in favor of Realm's tools?
CLARIFICATION.WHY: Determines whether the plugin removes or wraps host-native mutation tools, and whether those writes count as a residual risk.

OPTIONS.OPTION: Disable host writes in required mode — Built-in write and edit are removed when required mode is active, so all mutations go through Realm. Strictest option, depends on Omp allowing tool removal.
Keep host writes with a warning — Built-in tools stay available and the status bar warns about unsandboxed writes. Keeps the host workflow intact but leaves a known gap.
